principles.summary: Complexity arrives as many small dependencies and obscurities, so each small one matters.
The goal is a good design that also works; adding complexity to finish a task faster is not acceptable.
Spend a steady 10-20% of development time improving the design, in small increments.
The best modules hide a lot of functionality behind a small interface.
Design interfaces so the most common use is the simplest one; rarely used options should not cost common callers anything.
Each module should own a few design decisions that no other module needs to know.
When complexity is unavoidable, the module should absorb it so its users do not have to.
Build only the functionality needed today, behind an interface that does not encode today's single caller.
Keep a general mechanism free of code for one particular use; put that code with the use.
Adjacent layers should offer different abstractions; layers that mirror each other add interfaces without adding function.
Handle hard cases inside the module instead of exporting them as exceptions or configuration.
Define operations so that the normal behaviour covers the cases that would otherwise be errors; failing that, mask errors low or aggregate their handling high.
Sketch two or more substantially different designs before choosing one.
Comments carry what the code cannot say: abstractions, units, boundaries, invariants and reasons.
Optimise code for the people who read it, not for the person who writes it.
Grow a system one well-designed abstraction at a time, not one feature hack at a time.
Do similar things the same way and different things differently; follow existing conventions over personal preference.
Measure before changing code for speed, and keep only changes that measurably help or simplify.

red_flags.name: Shallow Module
red_flags.summary: The interface is nearly as complicated as the implementation it hides.
red_flags.ask: What does a caller avoid learning by using this instead of the code inside it?

red_flags.name: Information Leakage
red_flags.summary: One design decision is reflected in several modules, so changing it means changing all of them.
red_flags.ask: Which single module could own this knowledge?

red_flags.name: Temporal Decomposition
red_flags.summary: Modules follow the order operations happen in instead of the knowledge each one needs.
red_flags.ask: What knowledge does each step need, and do two steps need the same knowledge?

red_flags.name: Overexposure
red_flags.summary: Common use of an API requires learning about rarely used features.
red_flags.ask: Could the common call work with a default?

red_flags.name: Pass-Through Method
red_flags.summary: A method only forwards its arguments to another method with a similar signature.
red_flags.ask: Which class is responsible for this feature, and should callers reach it directly?

red_flags.name: Repetition
red_flags.summary: Nontrivial code appears in several places.
red_flags.ask: What abstraction would make this code exist once?

red_flags.name: Special-General Mixture
red_flags.summary: A general mechanism contains code for one particular use of it.
red_flags.ask: Can the special-purpose part move up to the code that needs it?

red_flags.name: Conjoined Methods
red_flags.summary: Two pieces of code can only be understood by reading both.
red_flags.ask: Should these be one method, or is the split in the wrong place?

red_flags.name: Comment Repeats Code
red_flags.summary: A comment says only what the adjacent code already says.
red_flags.ask: What does a reader need that the code does not show: units, boundaries, reasons?

red_flags.name: Implementation Documentation Contaminates Interface
red_flags.summary: An interface comment describes internals that callers do not need.
red_flags.ask: What must a caller know to use this, and nothing more?

red_flags.name: Vague Name
red_flags.summary: A name could refer to many things, so readers guess, and guess wrong.
red_flags.ask: Seen alone, what would a reader guess this name holds?

red_flags.name: Hard to Pick Name
red_flags.summary: No short precise name fits, which suggests the thing has no clean definition.
red_flags.ask: Is this one thing or several things sharing a variable?

red_flags.name: Hard to Describe
red_flags.summary: A complete description of a method or variable needs a long comment.
red_flags.ask: What would make the full description short?

red_flags.name: Nonobvious Code
red_flags.summary: A quick read does not reveal what the code does or means.
red_flags.ask: What information is the reader missing, and where should it live?

detectors.signal: The body is one call that passes the function's own parameters, in order, to a method of the same name on another object.
exempt: The method implements an interface or overrides a parent: checked by the binary.
A dispatcher chooses among callees: impossible with a one-statement body.
The call goes to super/parent, which is inheritance, not delegation: checked by the binary.
fix: Let callers use the lower object directly.
Move the feature so each class has distinct responsibilities.
Merge the two classes when they cannot be separated.

detectors.signal: Every content word (at least two) of the comment, or of a doc comment's first paragraph, also appears in the identifiers of the code it describes. String literal contents do not count as code.
exempt: Tool directives, license headers and section markers: checked by the binary.
Test files are skipped.
fix: Delete the comment.
Replace it with what the code does not say: units, boundary inclusivity, invariants, the reason the code exists.

detectors.signal: The interface comment of a public function or type names a private field, function or constant of the same file.
exempt: The private name is also a public concept with the same spelling: verify by reading.
fix: Describe the behaviour a caller observes; move implementation notes inside the body.

detectors.signal: A variable named `result` lives in a function that returns nothing.
exempt: The variable holds the result of the call on the line that declares it and is read right away: verify by reading.
Test files are skipped.
fix: Name the variable after what it holds, such as `mergedLine` or `totalChars`.

detectors.signal: A public method returns a private collection field (list, map, set, Vec, array) of its own object.
exempt: The type is a plain data record whose fields are its interface: verify by reading.
fix: Offer the operations callers need (`getParameter(name)`) instead of the container.

detectors.signal: A change edited a function's signature while leaving its interface comment untouched.
exempt: The comment still describes the new signature completely: verify by reading.
fix: Update the interface comment in the same change.

detectors.signal: A function of one statement and at most three lines that is called from exactly one place in the repository.
exempt: The function implements an interface or overrides a parent: checked by the binary.
The name hides a decision the caller should not know: verify by reading.
Framework entry points invoked by name from outside the code: verify by reading.
fix: Inline it at its only caller.

detectors.signal: An error handler discards the error of one call: an empty catch, `except: pass`, `let _ = f()` or `f().ok();`. One discard is enough to report. When several sites discard the same callee, the fix belongs in the callee's definition.
exempt: The callee must report this error to other callers: verify by reading.
The discarded value is not an error: verify by reading.
fix: Redefine the callee so this case is normal behaviour.
Mask the error inside the callee.
If the error matters, handle it.

detectors.signal: Statements of three or more code lines appear in two or more places with the same structure, names and literals aside.
exempt: Snippets of one or two lines are not reported: checked by the binary.
Extraction would need a long parameter list; the finding reports the identifier count.
Test files are skipped.
fix: Extract a function with a simple signature.
Restructure so the code runs in one place.

detectors.signal: Every call site of a function (at least three) passes the same literal in the same position.
exempt: The parameter exists for tests or for a known upcoming caller: verify by asking.
fix: Give the parameter a default or remove it.

detectors.signal: Two source files changed together in at least three commits and in at least half the commits of the less active file, yet neither imports the other nor calls a function the other defines.
exempt: A test and the file it tests.
A shared reason the code already documents in one place.
fix: Move the shared decision into one module.
If it cannot move, document it where both sides will see it.

detectors.signal: A generic name (`data`, `info`, `tmp`, `value`, `status`, a single letter) is used more than 25 lines away from its declaration.
exempt: Short loop indices whose whole range is visible.
Names the codebase uses consistently for one thing.
fix: Choose a name that says what the value is.

detectors.signal: A public function returns a tuple, so callers read its parts by position instead of by name.
exempt: The parts are named at every use by destructuring: verify by reading.
fix: Return a small named type whose fields say what each part is.

questions.text: What is the simplest interface that covers every current need?
In how many situations will this method be used?
Is this API easy to use for the needs we have today?
Does a caller need to know this to use the module?
Can callers choose a better value for this setting than the module can compute itself?
What is this code trying to do, and what is the simplest statement that explains all of it?
Could someone who has never seen the code write this comment by reading the code next to it?
Seen in isolation, how close would a reader's guess about this name be?
Is this split by the knowledge each part needs, or by the order things happen?
Do these pieces share information, get used together in both directions, overlap conceptually, or need each other to be understood?
If the system had been designed with this change in mind from the start, what would it look like?
Is there new information the old convention lacked, and is the new way worth updating every old use?
Which alternatives did we consider, and what would make a better one than all of them?
